The e2e framework does not support Playwright’s locator-composition methods such as `locator.and()` and `locator.or()`.

For nested selectors, use a single CSS selector with `locator()`, for example:

```ts
page.locator('.parent .child')
```

You can also use a supported locator method such as `getByRole()` or `getByTestId()` with a CSS selector where appropriate.

`browser.evaluate` is restricted to JSON-compatible inputs and outputs so values can be safely serialized between the test runner and the browser. This keeps the API predictable and avoids passing browser-specific objects—such as DOM nodes, functions, or cyclic structures—that cannot be reliably transferred or represented.

In Maestro, text taps and visibility checks are typically written as YAML commands such as `tapOn: "Continue"` and `runFlow` with `when: visible: "..."`. In e2e, use the corresponding API calls instead: tap a text locator and put conditional flow logic in code using a visibility check.

Text matching also changes: Maestro’s text commands generally match visible text, while e2e locators may use different matching rules (often exact by default). Specify the intended match explicitly—such as exact or partial matching—and scope the locator if needed to avoid ambiguous matches.

`expect(locator).toBeVisible()` retries until the element becomes visible or the assertion times out. `locator.isVisible()` checks immediately and returns `false` if the element is absent or hidden; it does not wait.

A baseline created earlier in the same run is treated as a new snapshot, not as an existing baseline.

- **Without `--update-snapshots`:** a later `toHaveScreenshot()` assertion does not use that newly written file as its baseline. A positive assertion fails because there was no baseline at the start of the run; a negated assertion passes.
- **With `--update-snapshots`:** the new baseline is used for later assertions in the run. A positive assertion can pass if the screenshot matches it; a negated assertion fails if it matches.

Under `on-all-retries`, trace pages preserve the trace for every attempt, including the initial run and each retry. Videos preserve only retry attempts, not the initial run. If the test is never retried, no video is retained under this policy, while its trace is retained.

Configure the budgets on each named agent’s configuration, rather than setting one shared value for the whole multi-worker run. Set the observation-size limit and model-input budget for every agent that needs them; workers can have different limits.

The run report records these budgets per named agent, alongside that agent’s run information. It does not represent them as a single aggregate budget for the multi-worker run.

An object containing only `specificationVersion`, `provider`, and `modelId` is a descriptor that identifies a model but lacks the live instance’s implementation and runtime capabilities.

`WORKER_EXIT` means the worker process exited unexpectedly; `WORKER_CRASH` means it crashed unexpectedly. In either case, the test file’s results from that worker are treated as failed or incomplete, while results from other workers and test files are preserved and can still be reported.

Register a dialog handler before triggering the action that opens the native JavaScript dialog. The handler must explicitly accept or dismiss it; if it does neither, the dialog remains open and the test will hang or time out.

Call `device.setPermission()` before `app.open()` so the permission is set before the app launches and requests it. This avoids relying on an in-app permission prompt, which may block or make the test nondeterministic.

Configuring `app.permissions` makes those permissions part of the app’s launch configuration. The framework reapplies them on subsequent app opens/restarts and when resetting app state, so the test can start from a clean state with the desired permissions already set.

When an `agent-device` command times out, the command is stopped, but the device or app may be left in an uncertain state. The next test attempt can then fail or behave unpredictably because it may inherit that state; reset or relaunch the app/device before retrying.

Only the two designated failure codes are allowed to be retryable because retrying is safe only for those specific, known failure conditions. If a different code claims retryability, the framework rejects it as invalid rather than retrying it.

Both capabilities depend on `observation` because they need the current state of the page to work correctly. `actions` uses it to decide what to interact with, while `location` uses it to identify or verify the current page or URL.

The runner does not impose a timeout on `prepare()` because provisioning may take an unpredictable amount of time—for example, while downloading dependencies or setting up the environment. A fixed timeout could terminate valid, slow provisioning.

For a web target, `prepare()` and `init()` receive the web app information, such as the app’s URL. For a device target, they receive the device app information, such as the app identifier or path.

During device warm-up, the framework launches the app with its configured launch arguments and permissions. Those are applied for the warm-up launch; they aren’t necessarily carried over to the later test launch.
